summary: This standards-track memo explains how to use SDP ANAT semantics in SIP. It defines the sdp-anat option-tag, which makes sure descriptions using ANAT are handled only by parties that understand it. It was replaced by RFC 5245.

eli5.summary: This document says how phone-call setups should signal that they offer several kinds of addresses. It was later replaced by RFC 5245.

questions: what is sdp anat in sip
how do dual stack devices offer addresses in sip
sip option tag for anat support
subtitle: Offering multiple network address types in phone call setup.

tldr.problem: In SIP (phone call setup), a device may support both IPv4 and IPv6. The Session Description Protocol (SDP) allows offering multiple address types in a single offer, but not all SIP endpoints understand this capability. Without a way to signal support for this feature, incompatible endpoints may misinterpret the offer.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4092 defines the sdp-anat SIP option-tag, which is placed in a Require header to indicate that the offer uses ANAT (Alternative Network Address Types). Only endpoints that support ANAT will process the offer.
tldr.outcome: Dual-stack and multi-stack devices can safely offer alternative network addresses without confusion. It was replaced by RFC 5245, which introduces a more comprehensive approach to interactive connectivity establishment.

today: RFC 4092 is obsoleted by RFC 5245, which introduces ICE (Interactive Connectivity Establishment), a more comprehensive framework for handling multiple address types and network conditions in SIP calls. ICE supersedes ANAT for practical deployment.

sections.title: Dual-Stack Device Offers
sections.content:
SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) is used to set up phone calls and other real-time communications. Many modern devices have both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. When such a device offers to start a call, it wants to say you can reach me at either of my addresses; pick one.

The Session Description Protocol (SDP) offers a way to do this through the ANAT (Alternative Network Address Types) semantics defined in RFC 4091. ANAT allows an offerer to group multiple media lines (one for each address type) and indicate that the answerer should choose one.

However, if the answerer does not understand ANAT, confusion results: it might accept all media lines (creating duplicate streams), or reject the offer without a clear error message. RFC 4092 solves this by defining the sdp-anat option-tag.
sections.eli5: When you call someone, you might say here is my IPv4 address and here is my IPv6 address, pick one. But if the other person does not understand that you are offering choices, they might get confused. This RFC solves that confusion.

sections.title: The sdp-anat Option-Tag
sections.content:
The sdp-anat option-tag is a SIP option-tag that can appear in Require and Supported header fields. An offerer that includes sdp-anat in a Require header is saying I am using ANAT; only answer if you understand it. A recipient that includes it in a Supported header is saying I understand ANAT.

SIP entities that support ANAT semantics MUST understand the sdp-anat option-tag. They understand what the grouping framework and ANAT specification say: that grouped media lines represent alternatives, and only one should be accepted.
sections.eli5: An option-tag is a label that says I am using a special feature. When you require sdp-anat, you are saying this offer uses ANAT, and you need to understand it.

sections.title: What Happens Without the Tag
sections.content:
Without the sdp-anat option-tag, answerers without ANAT support behave unpredictably. If an answerer supports all the address types in an offer but not ANAT, it might accept all media lines, wasting bandwidth by establishing multiple streams. Or it might reject the offer because it encounters unknown syntax, sending a confusing error message.

If an answerer does not support all address types, it might accept only the ones it understands (which is actually acceptable behavior) or reject the entire offer without clear explanation.

The sdp-anat option-tag prevents these scenarios. An answerer without ANAT support will reject the request with a 420 Bad Extension response, explicitly indicating that it does not support ANAT.
sections.eli5: Without the tag, a device that does not understand ANAT might accept all the address options (creating too many streams), or reject the call with a confusing error. The tag says only talk to me if you get this.

sections.title: Requirement and Discovery
sections.content:
Offerers that use ANAT semantics SHOULD place the sdp-anat option-tag in a Require header field of the SIP offer. This ensures that only answerers with ANAT support will receive the offer.

The option-tag also enables capability discovery. An endpoint can send a SIP OPTIONS request and include sdp-anat in a Require header. Only servers that support ANAT will respond with a 200 OK message. This allows clients to discover which servers in their domain support ANAT without trying to send a full SIP invitation.
sections.eli5: When you send a call offer using ANAT, you put sdp-anat in a Require header so only compatible devices will answer. You can also use OPTIONS requests to ask a server do you support ANAT? without making a real call.

sections.title: DoS and Tampering Risks
sections.content:
An attacker could add the sdp-anat option-tag to the Require header to cause a denial-of-service attack: if a UAS (User Agent Server) does not support ANAT, it will reject the request. Conversely, an attacker could remove the sdp-anat tag, causing multiple media streams to be established if the answerer does not understand ANAT.

To defend against these attacks, the RFC recommends integrity protection of the Require header field. The natural choice for SIP is S/MIME (Secure MIME), which cryptographically signs SIP message headers.
sections.eli5: An attacker could trick the sdp-anat tag into the message to break the call, or remove it to waste bandwidth. To prevent this, protect the Require header by signing it.
